title: 2024 Smart‑Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: The 2024 smart‑meter dataset comprises 1,428 readings with a total electricity consumption of 1,207,699.96 kWh (≈845.73 kWh per reading). Industrial use dominates (≈83% of total), while commercial and residential use are much smaller. Consumption peaks in the fourth quarter and rises modestly (4.71 %) in the second half of the year. Hot‑day commercial demand is low (19 readings, 415.29 kWh average). Energy use shows high variability (std ≈ 913 kWh) and a negative temperature‑consumption correlation for commercial meters (‑0.64). Peak tariffs represent just under half of total use, with 12 meters active and the highest‑use meter accounting for 252,241.26 kWh.

key_findings.statement: The dataset contains 1,428 readings with a total electricity consumption of 1,207,699.96 kWh, averaging 845.73 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings dominate consumption at 995,362.16 kWh, far exceeding Commercial (196,367.15 kWh) and Residential (15,970.65 kWh).
Quarterly consumption shows the highest use in Q4 (352,881.81 kWh) followed by Q1 (319,677.67 kWh), Q2 (270,277.36 kWh) and Q3 (264,863.12 kWh).
Second‑half consumption (617,744.93 kWh) is 4.71 % higher than the first half (589,955.03 kWh), indicating an increase.
On days with temperature ≥ 25 °C, the 19 Commercial readings averaged 415.29 kWh.

Across all readings, the median consumption is 406.8 kWh with a standard deviation of 913.44 kWh. The average temperature is 11.61 °C, with 62 missing temperature values. For Commercial meters, temperature and consumption are negatively correlated (‑0.64).
Peak tariffs account for 49.65 % of total use (599,624.07 kWh) versus 50.35 % off‑peak (608,075.89 kWh). Twelve distinct meters are recorded, and the single highest‑use meter consumed 252,241.26 kWh.

limitations: The data cover only the calendar year 2024 and may not reflect longer‑term trends.
Temperature readings are missing for 62 records, which could bias the temperature‑consumption analysis.
Only 12 distinct meters are present, limiting the generalisability of meter‑level insights.
Commercial temperature‑consumption correlation is based on a small subset of readings with valid temperatures.
conclusion: Electricity consumption in 2024 is heavily weighted toward industrial use, with a modest seasonal increase in the second half of the year and a clear quarterly pattern that peaks in Q4. Hot‑day commercial demand is low, and temperature appears to reduce commercial consumption. Tariff analysis shows a near‑even split between peak and off‑peak usage. Stakeholders should focus on industrial demand management, consider seasonal load‑shifting strategies, and address data gaps in temperature reporting to improve future analyses.
